::: {.solutions}

**Twenty-seven problems** across the four methods — **direct**, **cases**, **contradiction**,
**counterexample** — plus choosing the right one and spotting a flaw. Work them in **two fast batches**
(Part 1 + Part 2, then the longer Part 3), the way the session runs. **Part 3 is the hard tier** — the
questions that separate a 7 from a 9. Everything is argued in **English sentences**;
no symbols are required on Paper 2. Question types are drawn from **MAT, AMC, STEP** proof questions —
the same ideas, one notch harder.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Recall box.** algebra → **direct** · even/odd or ± → **cases** · "impossible / irrational / no
largest" → **contradiction** · a "for all" you doubt → **counterexample**. You can *disprove* a "for
all" with one example; you can never *prove* one that way.
:::

# Part 1 — Core methods, fast

## Question 1

::: {.question}
Prove that the sum of any two odd numbers is even.
:::

Write each odd number as $2k+1$ — [that makes the argument cover every odd number at once]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(direct)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$(2a+1)+(2b+1)=2(a+b+1)$, which is $2\times(\text{integer})$ — even. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Which single value disproves **"every prime number is odd"**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $2$ &nbsp; **C** $9$ &nbsp; **D** $15$
:::

A "for all" dies to one example fitting the hypothesis but breaking the conclusion.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample, MCQ)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** $2$ is prime but even. ($9,15$ are odd **and** not prime, so they are not counterexamples; $1$ is
not prime.) $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
What is the best method to prove **"$\sqrt2$ is irrational"**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** direct proof &nbsp; **B** proof by cases &nbsp; **C** proof by contradiction &nbsp;
**D** disproof by counterexample
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(choosing a method, MCQ)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** "Irrational" is a claim of impossibility (no fraction works) — contradiction is the natural weapon:
assume it *is* rational and force an absurdity. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
To prove by contradiction that **there is no largest positive integer**, what do you assume first?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** every integer is small &nbsp; **B** there **is** a largest positive integer $N$ &nbsp;
**C** $N+1$ is largest &nbsp; **D** there are infinitely many integers
:::

Contradiction opens with the **exact negation** of the goal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(contradiction, MCQ)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** Assume a largest positive integer $N$ exists; then $N+1$ is larger — contradiction. (**D** is the
conclusion, not the assumption.) $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
Prove that $\lvert x\rvert \ge x$ for every real number $x$.
:::

Split at the sign of $x$ — [two exhaustive cases]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(cases)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**Case $x\ge0$:** $\lvert x\rvert=x$, so $\lvert x\rvert\ge x$. **Case $x<0$:** $\lvert x\rvert=-x>0>x$,
so $\lvert x\rvert> x$. Both cases give $\lvert x\rvert\ge x$. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 6

::: {.question}
Disprove: **"for all real $a,b$, if $a<b$ then $a^2<b^2$."**
:::

[Test negatives]{.hl} — squaring can reverse an inequality.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$a=-3$, $b=2$: then $a<b$ holds, but $a^2=9>4=b^2$. One counterexample disproves it. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 7

::: {.question}
Prove that if $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is even.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(direct)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n=2k\Rightarrow n^2=4k^2=2(2k^2)$ — even. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 8

::: {.question}
A student writes: *"$n^2+n$ is even because $1^2+1=2$, $2^2+2=6$, $3^2+3=12$ are all even, so it holds for
all $n$."* The conclusion is true, but why is this not a proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** the sums are wrong &nbsp; **B** examples cannot prove a "for all" &nbsp;
**C** the statement is false &nbsp; **D** nothing — it is valid
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(spot the flaw, MCQ)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** A finite list leaves infinitely many $n$ unchecked. A real proof: $n^2+n=n(n+1)$ is a product of
two consecutive integers, one even. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 2 — Constructing proofs (exam standard)

## Question 9

::: {.question}
Prove that the product of two consecutive integers is even.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(direct / cases)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
Take $n$ and $n+1$. One of any two consecutive integers is even, so their product $n(n+1)$ is even. (Or:
if $n=2k$, product $=2k(n+1)$; if $n=2k+1$, then $n+1=2k+2$ is even.) $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 10

::: {.question}
Prove that if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even.
:::

Assume the **opposite** of the conclusion.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(contradiction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
Suppose $n^2$ even but $n$ **odd**. Then $n=2k+1$, so $n^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$ — **odd**,
contradicting $n^2$ even. So $n$ is even. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 11

::: {.question}
Prove that the square of any integer is of the form $4k$ or $4k+1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(cases)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**Even $n=2m$:** $n^2=4m^2$ (form $4k$). **Odd $n=2m+1$:** $n^2=4m^2+4m+1=4(m^2+m)+1$ (form $4k+1$).
Exhaustive, so it holds for all $n$. $\;\blacksquare$

*Consequence: a perfect square is never $4k+2$ or $4k+3$.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 12

::: {.question}
Prove that if $n$ is an odd integer, then $n^2-1$ is divisible by $8$.
:::

Factor $n^2-1=(n-1)(n+1)$; [among two consecutive even numbers one is a multiple of $4$]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(direct)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n=2k+1\Rightarrow n^2-1=(2k)(2k+2)=4k(k+1)$. Since $k,k+1$ are consecutive, one is even, so $k(k+1)=2m$;
hence $n^2-1=8m$. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 13

::: {.question}
Prove that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(contradiction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
Let $r$ rational, $x$ irrational; suppose $r+x=s$ is rational. Then $x=s-r$ is a difference of two
rationals, hence rational — contradicting $x$ irrational. So $r+x$ is irrational. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 14

::: {.question}
Disprove: **"$2^{n}-1$ is prime for every integer $n\ge2$."**
:::

Test the values a hopeful pattern skips.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n=4$: $2^4-1=15=3\times5$, not prime. Counterexample. $\;\blacksquare$

**Why we look for a composite value — and where to find it.** To disprove "**always** prime" you only need
**one** $n$ for which $2^n-1$ is **composite** (not prime). The trick is *which* $n$ to try: take a
**composite exponent** $n=ab$, because such a power *always* factors:
$$2^{ab}-1=(2^{a}-1)\bigl(2^{a(b-1)}+2^{a(b-2)}+\dots+1\bigr).$$
So $n=4=2\times2$ is guaranteed to have $2^{2}-1=3$ as a factor — hence $2^4-1=15$ is a multiple of $3$,
no calculation needed; and $n=6=2\times3$ gives $2^6-1=63=7\times9$. A **prime** exponent need not fail
($2^3-1=7$ and $2^5-1=31$ are prime), which is exactly why testing $n=1,2,3,\dots$ in order looks
hopeful — so **skip the prime exponents and test a composite one**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 15

::: {.question}
Prove, by cases, that $n^2+3n$ is even for every integer $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(cases)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**Even $n=2k$:** $4k^2+6k=2(2k^2+3k)$. **Odd $n=2k+1$:** $(2k+1)^2+3(2k+1)=4k^2+10k+4=2(2k^2+5k+2)$. Both
even; exhaustive. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 16

::: {.question}
A student claims **"$n^2+n+41$ is prime for every positive integer $n$."** Disprove it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n=40$: $40^2+40+41=1681=41^2$, not prime. Counterexample. $\;\blacksquare$

*Checking small $n$ (all prime) proves nothing — the value at $n=40$ is forced to have factor $41$.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}

# Part 3 — Push to 8–9 (harder, cross-exam)

## Question 17

::: {.question}
Prove, by contradiction, that $\sqrt3$ is irrational. You may use: **if $m^2$ is divisible by $3$ then
$m$ is divisible by $3$.**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(contradiction — MAT/STEP)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
Suppose $\sqrt3=\dfrac{a}{b}$ in lowest terms. Then $a^2=3b^2$, so $3$ divides $a^2$, hence $3$ divides $a$; write
$a=3c$. Then $9c^2=3b^2\Rightarrow b^2=3c^2$, so $3$ divides $b$. Now $3$ divides both $a$ and $b$ —
contradicting "lowest terms". So $\sqrt3$ is irrational. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 18

::: {.question}
Prove that $n^3-n$ is divisible by $6$ for every integer $n$.
:::

Factor into consecutive integers, then argue divisibility by $2$ **and** by $3$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(cases / direct — STEP)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n^3-n=n(n^2-1)=(n-1)\,n\,(n+1)$ — three **consecutive** integers. Among any three consecutive integers
one is a multiple of $3$, and at least one is even, so the product is divisible by both $3$ and $2$, hence
by $6$. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 19

::: {.question}
Decide whether **"if $p$ and $q$ are prime then $p+q$ is even"** is true; if false, disprove it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample — AMC)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**False.** $p=2$, $q=3$ are prime but $p+q=5$ is odd. The claim quietly assumes both primes are odd, but
$2$ is the even prime. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 20

::: {.question}
Prove that there is no smallest positive rational number.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(contradiction)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
Suppose $q$ is the smallest positive rational. Then $\dfrac{q}{2}$ is also a positive rational and
$\dfrac{q}{2}<q$ — smaller than the supposed smallest. Contradiction, so no smallest positive rational
exists. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 21

::: {.question}
A "proof" that $2=1$: *Let $a=b$. Then $a^2=ab$, so $a^2-b^2=ab-b^2$, i.e. $(a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b)$. Dividing
by $(a-b)$ gives $a+b=b$, so $2b=b$, hence $2=1$.* Where is the error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a^2=ab$ is wrong &nbsp; **B** the factorisation is wrong &nbsp;
**C** dividing by $(a-b)$, which is $0$ &nbsp; **D** $2b=b$ does not give $2=1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(spot the flaw — MAT-style)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** Since $a=b$, $a-b=0$, and dividing by $0$ is not allowed — that step is invalid. Every other line
is correct. $\;\blacksquare$

*The classic Err2 trap: cancelling a factor that might be (here, definitely is) zero.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 22

::: {.question}
Disprove: **"the sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational."**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample — STEP)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$\sqrt2$ and $2-\sqrt2$ are both irrational, but their sum is $\sqrt2+(2-\sqrt2)=2$, which is rational.
Counterexample. (Simplest: $\sqrt2+(-\sqrt2)=0$.) $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 23

::: {.question}
Prove that $\log_2 3$ is irrational.
:::

Assume it is rational, clear to an **integer power equation**, then compare parities.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(contradiction — STEP/olympiad)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — contradiction; an even-vs-odd clash
:::

Suppose $\log_2 3=\dfrac{a}{b}$ with positive integers $a,b$. Then $2^{a/b}=3$, so $2^{a}=3^{b}$. But
$2^{a}$ is **even** (as $a\ge1$) while $3^{b}$ is **odd** — impossible. So $\log_2 3$ is irrational.
$\;\blacksquare$

*The contradiction is a parity clash: an even number cannot equal an odd number.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4.5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 24

::: {.question}
Prove that if $a^2+b^2$ is divisible by $4$, then $a$ and $b$ are both even.
:::

Use the earlier fact that every square is $4k$ (even) or $4k+1$ (odd), and check the three parity
combinations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(cases — harder)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — cases via squares mod 4
:::

A square is $4k$ if the base is even and $4k+1$ if odd. So, working modulo $4$:

- both even: $0+0=0$ ✓ (divisible by $4$);
- one odd: $0+1=1$;
- both odd: $1+1=2$.

Only "both even" gives a multiple of $4$. Hence if $4$ divides $a^2+b^2$, then $a$ and $b$ are both even.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 25

::: {.question}
Disprove: **"$n!+1$ is prime for every positive integer $n$."**
:::

The first few work — test a little further.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(counterexample — harder)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n=1,2,3$ give $2,3,7$ (all prime), but $n=4$: $4!+1=25=5^2$, not prime. Counterexample. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 26

::: {.question}
Prove that $n^3$ and $n$ always have the **same parity** (both odd, or both even).
:::

Show their **difference** is even.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(direct — harder)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
$n^3-n=(n-1)\,n\,(n+1)$, a product of three consecutive integers, which is even. Since $n^3-n$ is even,
$n^3$ and $n$ differ by an even number, so they have the same parity. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 27

::: {.question}
To solve $\sqrt{x+2}=x$, a student squares both sides: $x+2=x^2\Rightarrow x^2-x-2=0\Rightarrow
(x-2)(x+1)=0$, so $x=2$ or $x=-1$ — and gives **both**. What is wrong?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** the factorisation is wrong &nbsp; **B** $x=-1$ does not satisfy the original equation —
squaring introduced it &nbsp; **C** $x=2$ is wrong &nbsp; **D** nothing
:::

Squaring can create **extraneous** roots — always check answers in the **original** equation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(spot the flaw — squaring, MCQ)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — the "squaring both sides" trap (Err2)
:::

**B.** Check: $x=2$ gives $\sqrt4=2$ ✓; but $x=-1$ gives $\sqrt1=1\neq-1$ ✗. Squaring both sides can
introduce a root that does not satisfy the original equation, so $x=-1$ must be rejected. Only $x=2$ is a
solution. $\;\blacksquare$

*Squaring is not reversible — it can turn a false statement into a true one, so every squared solution
must be tested in the original.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
# Part 4 — Exam bank: mock papers

One counterexample kills a "for all" claim, and the exam knows it: every question in Parts 4 and 5 hands
you a short list of candidates and asks **which of them actually work**. The whole skill is checking a candidate against
**both** halves of the claim — the hypothesis *and* the conclusion — instead of only the part that catches
the eye.

::: {.callout-important}
## What makes a counterexample

To disprove *"if $H$ then $C$"*, you need one case where
$$H \text{ is \textbf{true}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\text{ is \textbf{false}} .$$

**Both conditions, every time.** A case where $H$ is false proves nothing — it is simply outside what the
claim ever said. *That is the single most common wrong answer in this part:* candidates pick the value that
makes the conclusion fail without noticing it was never covered by the hypothesis.
:::

---

## Question 28 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set A · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement: *no positive integer $N$ that is less than $20$ can be written as the sum of two
non-prime integers that are greater than $1$.*

Which of the following is a counterexample to this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $N=8$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $N=13$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $N=24$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I and II only &nbsp; **C** II and III only &nbsp;
**D** I and III only &nbsp; **E** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Easy — but read the range)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** The non-prime integers greater than $1$ start $4,6,8,9,10,12,14,15,16,18,\dots$

- **I, $N=8$:** $8=4+4$, and $4$ is non-prime and $>1$. Also $8<20$. **Counterexample ✓**
- **II, $N=13$:** $13=4+9$, both non-prime and $>1$. Also $13<20$. **Counterexample ✓**
- **III, $N=24$:** it can certainly be written that way ($24=4+20=6+18=8+16=\dots$) — **but $24$ is not less
  than $20$**, so it is not a case the statement ever claimed anything about. **Not a counterexample ✗**

*This is the trap in its purest form.* $N=24$ satisfies the interesting half and fails the boring half. A
counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis — here "$N<20$" — before anything else matters.

**Note also that $13$ is odd**, which catches people who assume two non-primes must give an even sum.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 29 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement: *if a positive integer $N$ has the property that $N^{2}$ is divisible by
$9$, then $N$ is divisible by $6$.*

Which of the following is a counterexample to this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $N=15$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $N=18$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $N=21$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** II and III only &nbsp; **G** I and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — tabulate both columns)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G.** Check each candidate against **both** halves:

| $N$ | $N^{2}$ | $9\mid N^{2}$ ? (hypothesis) | $6\mid N$ ? (conclusion) | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $15$ | $225$ | yes | **no** | **✓** |
| $18$ | $324$ | yes | yes | ✗ — the claim holds here |
| $21$ | $441$ | yes | **no** | **✓** |

So I and III only.

*Why the claim is false in general:* $9\mid N^{2}$ forces $3\mid N$, but it says nothing about the factor
$2$ that "divisible by $6$" also demands. Every odd multiple of $3$ — $3,9,15,21,27,\dots$ — is a
counterexample, so the two offered are not special.

**Note $N=18$ is included deliberately:** it satisfies the hypothesis *and* the conclusion, so the claim is
simply **true** for it. A case where a claim holds can never be a counterexample. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 30 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement: *if a positive integer $N$ has the property that $N^{2}$ is divisible by
$12$, then $N$ is divisible by $12$.*

Which of the following are counterexamples to this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $N=6$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $N=8$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $N=18$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **IV** $N=24$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** I and III only
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — the same table, one step harder)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D.**

| $N$ | $N^{2}$ | $12\mid N^{2}$ ? | $12\mid N$ ? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $6$ | $36$ | yes | **no** | **✓** |
| $8$ | $64$ | **no** ($64=12\times5+4$) | no | ✗ — hypothesis fails |
| $18$ | $324$ | yes ($324=12\times27$) | **no** | **✓** |
| $24$ | $576$ | yes | yes | ✗ — claim holds |

*Each wrong option fails for a different reason,* which is why this question separates candidates so well:
$N=8$ never enters the discussion, and $N=24$ is a case where the claim is true.

**Where the claim goes wrong.** $12=2^{2}\times3$, so $12\mid N^{2}$ needs $N^{2}$ to carry $2^{2}$ and $3$ —
which only forces $N$ to carry $2$ and $3$, i.e. $6\mid N$. The extra factor of $2$ is not implied.
*Compare with Q29:* same structure, $9=3^{2}$ in place of $12=2^{2}\cdot3$. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 31 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement &nbsp;$(*)$&nbsp; *every prime number $n$ can be written as the sum of $2$ square
numbers.*

How many counterexamples to $(*)$ are there in the range $0<n<40$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $2$ &nbsp; **B** $3$ &nbsp; **C** $4$ &nbsp; **D** $5$ &nbsp; **E** $6$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — count, do not just find one)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**E — six.** The squares available are $1,4,9,16,25,36$. Go through every prime below $40$:

| $n$ | as a sum of two squares | | $n$ | as a sum of two squares |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $2$ | $1+1$ ✓ | | $17$ | $1+16$ ✓ |
| $3$ | — **✗** | | $19$ | — **✗** |
| $5$ | $1+4$ ✓ | | $23$ | — **✗** |
| $7$ | — **✗** | | $29$ | $4+25$ ✓ |
| $11$ | — **✗** | | $31$ | — **✗** |
| $13$ | $4+9$ ✓ | | $37$ | $1+36$ ✓ |

The failures are $3,7,11,19,23,31$ — **six** of them.

*The pattern behind the answer* (worth seeing, though the exam only wants the count): the primes that **do**
work are $2$ and those of the form $4k+1$; those that fail are exactly the primes of the form $4k+3$. Check:
$3,7,11,19,23,31$ all leave remainder $3$ on division by $4$.

**The exam skill here is different from Q28–Q30.** Those asked *is this one a counterexample?*; this asks
*how many are there?* — so you must be systematic, not lucky. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

:::

## Question 32 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement: *if $f'(x)>0$ for all real $x$, then $f(x+1)>f(x)$ for all real $x$.*

Which function provides a counterexample?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(x)=4^{x}$ &nbsp; **B** $f(x)=4x^{2}+1$ &nbsp; **C** $f(x)=4x^{3}$ &nbsp;
**D** $f(x)=\dfrac{4-x}{x}$ &nbsp; **E** $f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{4x}$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — the counterexample lives at the asymptote)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**E.** Again both halves must hold: **$f'>0$** *and* **$f(x+1)>f(x)$ fails somewhere**.

| | $f$ | $f'$ | hypothesis $f'>0$? | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | $4^{x}$ | $4^{x}\ln4$ | yes | increasing everywhere, so the conclusion holds — ✗ |
| **B** | $4x^{2}+1$ | $8x$ | **no** ($f'<0$ for $x<0$) | hypothesis fails — ✗ |
| **C** | $4x^{3}$ | $12x^{2}$ | **no** ($f'(0)=0$) | hypothesis fails — ✗ |
| **D** | $\dfrac{4}{x}-1$ | $-\dfrac{4}{x^{2}}$ | **no** — always *negative* | hypothesis fails — ✗ |
| **E** | $\dfrac14-\dfrac{1}{4x}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4x^{2}}$ | **yes**, wherever defined | **✓** |

For **E**, take $x=-\tfrac12$:
$$f\left(-\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14+\tfrac12=\tfrac34,\qquad
f\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14-\tfrac12=-\tfrac14 ,$$
so $f(x+1)<f(x)$ — the conclusion fails.

*How can a function with a positive gradient everywhere decrease?* Because it is **not defined everywhere**.
$f$ has a vertical asymptote at $x=0$: it rises on $(-\infty,0)$ and rises again on $(0,\infty)$, but it
**drops from $+$ to $-$ across the gap**. "Increasing on each piece" is not "increasing", and the step from
$-\tfrac12$ to $\tfrac12$ jumps that gap.

**The lesson.** Whenever a claim says "for all real $x$", check the *domain* first. Option **D** is placed
there to catch the opposite slip — it has the asymptote but the wrong sign of gradient, so it never satisfies
the hypothesis at all. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 5 — Exam bank: real past papers

Seven genuine TMUA papers. Counterexample is one of the two most stable slots on the whole test — about two
questions a year in every sitting from 2016 to 2023 — and the exam asks for it in four recognisable ways:

1. **Which of these candidates works?** (2018 Q3, 2023 Q3) — check each against *both* halves of the claim.
2. **Which statement can this one fact disprove?** (2019 Q7) — the fact is fixed; the claim varies.
3. **Which function is a counterexample?** (2017 Q16) — the hypothesis is itself something to verify.
4. **Is this disproof valid?** (2020 Q8) — and sometimes the honest answer is *yes*.

[The recurring wrong answer is a candidate that breaks the conclusion but never satisfied the
hypothesis]{.hl}, so it was never covered by the claim at all. Check the hypothesis first, every time.


## Question 33 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q6 &nbsp;◆</span>

::: {.question}
Which function is a **counterexample** to the claim *"if $f'(x)>0$ for all real $x$, then $f(x)>0$ for all
real $x$"*?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $x^{2}+1$ &nbsp; **B** $x^{2}-1$ &nbsp; **C** $x^{3}+x+1$ &nbsp; **D** $1-x$ &nbsp;
**E** $2^{x}$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a real TMUA question; both halves again)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** You need a function that **is increasing everywhere** (hypothesis true) yet **dips below zero**
somewhere (conclusion false).

For $f(x)=x^{3}+x+1$: $f'(x)=3x^{2}+1$, which is $\ge1>0$ for every real $x$ — so the hypothesis holds. But
$f(-2)=-8-2+1=-9<0$, so the conclusion fails. **Counterexample ✓**

| | $f$ | $f'$ | hypothesis? | conclusion? | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | $x^{2}+1$ | $2x$ | **no** — negative for $x<0$ | true anyway | ✗ |
| **B** | $x^{2}-1$ | $2x$ | **no** — negative for $x<0$ | false | ✗ — *hypothesis fails* |
| **C** | $x^{3}+x+1$ | $3x^{2}+1$ | **yes** | **false** at $x=-2$ | **✓** |
| **D** | $1-x$ | $-1$ | **no** — decreasing | false | ✗ |
| **E** | $2^{x}$ | $2^{x}\ln2$ | **yes** | **true** — always positive | ✗ — *claim holds* |

**B is the trap.** $x^{2}-1$ does go negative, which is the eye-catching half — but its gradient is negative
for $x<0$, so it was never a case the claim covered. *A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis first.*

**And E is the other trap**, for the opposite reason: it satisfies the hypothesis but the claim is true for
it. Only C fails the claim while obeying its hypothesis.

*Why the claim is false in general:* $f'>0$ controls the **direction** a function moves, never its
**height**. Any increasing function can be slid downwards — $x^{3}+x+1$ is just $x^{3}+x$ shifted, and it
runs to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ however it is shifted. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Question 33 · y = x³ + x + 1 rises everywhere (f' = 3x² + 1 > 0) yet is negative to the left of x ≈ −0.68 — the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = np.linspace(-2.2, 1.5, 500); y = x**3 + x + 1
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.6))
ax.fill_between(x, y, 0, where=(y < 0), color='#d62728', alpha=0.15)
ax.plot(x, y, color='#1f77b4', lw=2.2, label=r'$y=x^{3}+x+1$')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9); ax.axvline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9)
r = -0.682327803
ax.plot([r], [0], 'o', color='#d62728', zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r'crosses zero at $x\approx-0.68$', xy=(r, 0), xytext=(-2.1, 2.6),
            color='#d62728', fontsize=9,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#d62728', lw=1))
ax.plot([-2], [-9], 'o', color='#d62728', zorder=5)
ax.annotate(r'$f(-2)=-9<0$', xy=(-2, -9), xytext=(-1.55, -7.4), color='#d62728', fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title(r"increasing everywhere, but not always positive", fontsize=11)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='lower right')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

## Question 34 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q16 &nbsp;◆</span>

::: {.question}
A sequence is given by $u_{1}=a$, $u_{2}=b$ and $u_{n+2}=u_{n}+u_{n+1}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive
integers with $\gcd(a,b)=7$. Which of the following **must** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $u_{2023}$ is a multiple of $7$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; if $u_{1}$ is not a factor of $u_{2}$, then $u_{1}$ is not a factor of $u_{n}$ for
any $n>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $\gcd(u_{1},u_{5})=7$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a real TMUA question; one proof and two counterexamples)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B — I only.** *"Must be true" makes each statement a "for all $a,b$" claim, so each is settled either by a
proof covering every case or by a single counterexample.* Here one of each, twice over.

**I — true, and it needs a proof.** $\gcd(a,b)=7$ means $7$ divides **both** $a$ and $b$. A sum of two
multiples of $7$ is a multiple of $7$, so $u_{3}=u_{1}+u_{2}$ is one; and then $u_{4}$, and so on. By
induction every term is a multiple of $7$ — including $u_{2023}$. *(Notice how little the index matters: the
$2023$ is decoration.)*

**III — false, by counterexample.** Expanding, $u_{5}=2a+3b$, so
$$\gcd(u_{1},u_{5})=\gcd(a,\,2a+3b)=\gcd(a,3b),$$
which need not be $7$. **Take $a=21$, $b=7$** (indeed $\gcd=7$): the sequence is $21,7,28,35,63$, and
$\gcd(21,63)=\mathbf{21}\neq7$. *The factor of $3$ shared by $21$ and $3b$ is what breaks it.*

**II — false, by counterexample.** **Take $a=14$, $b=7$**: the sequence is $14,7,21,28,49$. Here $u_{1}=14$
does **not** divide $u_{2}=7$, so the hypothesis holds — but $u_{4}=28$ **is** divisible by $14$, so the
conclusion fails. *The reason is visible in $u_{4}=a+2b$: the coefficient $2$ can supply exactly the factor
that $b$ alone was missing.*

**The method, not the arithmetic.** Three statements, and the right first question for each is *"am I being
asked to prove this for every $a,b$, or to break it with one pair?"* Statements II and III are both of the
shape "this always happens", so **one** well-chosen pair ends each — and small multiples of $7$ are where to
look, because they keep $\gcd(a,b)=7$ while letting an extra common factor sneak in downstream.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 35 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement:

> A car journey consists of two parts. In the first part, the average speed is $u$ km/h. In the second
> part, the average speed is $v$ km/h. Hence the average speed for the whole journey is
> $\tfrac12(u+v)$ km/h.

Which of the following examples of car journeys provide(s) a **counterexample** to the statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $50$ km/h for $100$ km, then $40$ km/h for $100$ km.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $50$ km/h for **one hour**, then $40$ km/h for **one hour**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $50$ km/h for $80$ km, then $40$ km/h for $100$ km.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

Average speed is **total distance over total time** — never the average of two speeds. [Read each option
for whether the two parts are matched by *distance* or by *time*]{.hl}, because that single difference
decides all three.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — testing candidates one at a time; the case that is *not* a counterexample is the point
:::

**F — I and III only.**

The claimed answer in every case is $\tfrac12(50+40)=45$ km/h.

| | distance | time | total | average speed | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | $100+100=200$ | $\tfrac{100}{50}+\tfrac{100}{40}=2+2.5=4.5$ | | $\dfrac{200}{4.5}=44.\dot4$ | **yes**, $\neq45$ |
| **II** | $50+40=90$ | $1+1=2$ | | $\dfrac{90}{2}=45$ | **no** — the claim holds |
| **III** | $80+100=180$ | $\tfrac{80}{50}+\tfrac{100}{40}=1.6+2.5=4.1$ | | $\dfrac{180}{4.1}=43.90\ldots$ | **yes**, $\neq45$ |

### Why II is the interesting one

*When the two parts take **equal times**, the mean of the speeds is exactly right.* The formula
$\tfrac12(u+v)$ is the time-weighted average, so it is correct precisely when the weights are equal. Option
II is built to be the case where the false claim happens to be true.

### Why I fails

Equal **distances**, not equal times — and the slower leg takes longer, so it gets more weight. The correct
value is the harmonic mean,

$$\frac{2uv}{u+v}=\frac{2\times50\times40}{90}=44.\dot4 ,$$

which is always **less** than $\tfrac12(u+v)$ unless $u=v$.

**The lesson.** A claim that is false in general can still be true in special cases, and [the exam always
includes one such case among the candidates]{.hl} — it is the commonest way to lose the mark. Test every
candidate; do not stop at the first one that works. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 36 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the claim:

> For all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$, &nbsp; $\sqrt{x^{y}}=x^{\sqrt y}$

Which of the following is/are a **counterexample** to the claim?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $x=1,\ y=16$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** &nbsp; $x=2,\ y=8$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** &nbsp; $x=3,\ y=4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

Do not try to decide whether the claim is true — [just evaluate the two sides at each of the three
pairs]{.hl}. Two of them are chosen so that a false claim comes out true, and spotting *why* is the whole
question.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a false claim with accidental successes; $\sqrt{x^{y}}=x^{y/2}$, not $x^{\sqrt y}$
:::

**C — II only.**

The left side is $\sqrt{x^{y}}=x^{y/2}$. So the claim is really

$$x^{y/2}=x^{\sqrt y}\;,$$

which for $x\neq1$ needs $\dfrac y2=\sqrt y$, i.e. $y=2\sqrt y$, i.e. $y=0$ or $y=4$.
*So the claim holds only when $x=1$ or $y=4$ — and both escape routes are on the candidate list.*

| | left $=x^{y/2}$ | right $=x^{\sqrt y}$ | equal? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** $x=1,y=16$ | $1^{8}=1$ | $1^{4}=1$ | ✓ | **no** — every power of $1$ is $1$ |
| **II** $x=2,y=8$ | $2^{4}=16$ | $2^{\sqrt8}=2^{2.828\ldots}=7.10\ldots$ | ✗ | **yes** |
| **III** $x=3,y=4$ | $3^{2}=9$ | $3^{\sqrt4}=3^{2}=9$ | ✓ | **no** — $y=4$ makes $\tfrac y2=\sqrt y$ |

Only II breaks it, so the answer is **C**.

**The lesson.** [A single counterexample disproves a "for all" claim, but a single agreement proves
nothing]{.hl} — and in this question two of the three candidates agree, for two *different* structural
reasons: $x=1$ kills the exponent, and $y=4$ is the one value where $\tfrac y2$ and $\sqrt y$ coincide.
*Simplify the claim before testing, and those two escape routes are visible in a line.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 37 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
For which one of the following statements can the fact that $12^{2}+16^{2}=20^{2}$ be used to produce a
**counterexample**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; If $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers which satisfy $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$, and the three numbers have **no common divisor**, then two of them are odd and the other is even.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; The equation $a^{4}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ has no solutions for which $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; The equation $a^{4}+b^{4}=c^{4}$ has no solutions for which $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; If $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers which satisfy $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$, then one is the **arithmetic mean** of the other two.
:::

The fact is fixed and the claim varies, so this is the counterexample test run four times. For each option
ask the two questions in order: **does $12,16,20$ satisfy the hypothesis**, and **does it break the
conclusion?** [You are also allowed to rewrite the fact]{.hl} — $144$, $256$ and $400$ can be presented in
more than one shape.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — one fact, four claims; and a counterexample you have to *construct* from the fact
:::

**B.**

The fact: $12^{2}+16^{2}=144+256=400=20^{2}$ ✓

### A — the hypothesis fails

The claim only covers triples with **no common divisor**, and $\gcd(12,16,20)=4$. *So $12,16,20$ lies
outside the claim entirely and can say nothing about it.* This is the classic trap: the conclusion does
fail here (two of $12,16,20$ are even, not odd), which makes A look right until the hypothesis is checked.

### B — a counterexample, once you rewrite the fact

B says $a^{4}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ is unsolvable. We need a **fourth** power. Note

$$256=16^{2}=4^{4},$$

so the same arithmetic reads

$$4^{4}+12^{2}=256+144=400=20^{2} .$$

With $a=4$, $b=12$, $c=20$ all positive integers, the claim is destroyed. ✓ *The fact was not handed over
in the right costume — recognising $16^{2}$ as $4^{4}$ is the work.*

### C — the fact cannot be reshaped that far

$a^{4}+b^{4}=c^{4}$ needs **both** $144$ and $256$ to be fourth powers, and $144=12^{2}$ is not:
$\sqrt{12}$ is irrational. *(This is Fermat's Last Theorem for $n=4$; no counterexample exists at all.)*

### D — the conclusion holds

$$\tfrac12(12+20)=16 ,$$

so $16$ **is** the arithmetic mean of the other two. The triple satisfies both the hypothesis and the
conclusion, so it supports D rather than refuting it. *(D is false in general — $3,4,5$ has no such mean —
but this fact is not the counterexample for it.)*

**The lesson.** Two different failures are on display here, and both are worth naming. [A candidate outside
the hypothesis is not a counterexample]{.hl} (option A), and [a candidate that satisfies the conclusion is
not one either]{.hl} (option D). Between them they account for most lost marks in this slot — and option B
adds a third demand: *the fact may need rewriting before it fits the claim.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 38 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement:

> $(*)$ &nbsp; **If** $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is an integer for every integer $x$, **then** $\mathrm{f}'(x)$ is an
> integer for every integer $x$.

Which one of the following is a **counterexample** to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)=\dfrac{x^{3}+x+1}{4}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)=\dfrac{x^{4}+x^{2}+x}{2}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)=\dfrac{x^{4}+x^{3}+x^{2}+x}{2}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)=\dfrac{x^{4}+2x^{3}+x^{2}}{4}$
:::

Two things must hold: $\mathrm{f}$ takes integer values at **every** integer (the hypothesis), and
$\mathrm{f}'$ fails to at **some** integer (the conclusion breaks). [Test the hypothesis first — it is much
cheaper]{.hl}, because $x=1$ disposes of any option whose numerator is odd there.

The tool for the hypothesis is that **$x(x+1)$ is always even**, so anything of that shape divided by $2$
is an integer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis; consecutive-integer divisibility
:::

**C.**

### Step 1 — which options even satisfy the hypothesis?

| | $\mathrm{f}(1)$ | hypothesis? |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $\dfrac{1+1+1}{4}=\dfrac34$ | ✗ not an integer — **out** |
| **B** | $\dfrac{1+1+1}{2}=\dfrac32$ | ✗ not an integer — **out** |
| **C** | $\dfrac{1+1+1+1}{2}=2$ | ✓ so far |
| **D** | $\dfrac{1+2+1}{4}=1$ | ✓ so far |

*Two options eliminated by a single substitution, before any differentiation.*

### Step 2 — do C and D really satisfy it for **every** integer?

**C.** &nbsp; $x^{4}+x^{3}+x^{2}+x=x\left(x^{2}+1\right)(x+1)$, and $x(x+1)$ is a product of consecutive
integers, hence even. So $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is an integer for every integer $x$ ✓

**D.** &nbsp; $x^{4}+2x^{3}+x^{2}=x^{2}(x+1)^{2}$, so

$$\mathrm{f}(x)=\left(\frac{x(x+1)}{2}\right)^{2},$$

and $\tfrac{x(x+1)}{2}$ is an integer — it is the triangular number. ✓

### Step 3 — the derivatives

**C.** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}'(x)=\dfrac{4x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x+1}{2}$. At $x=2$:

$$\mathrm{f}'(2)=\frac{32+12+4+1}{2}=\frac{49}{2},$$

**not an integer.** Hypothesis holds, conclusion fails — **C is the counterexample.** ✓

*(Note $\mathrm{f}'(1)=\tfrac{10}{2}=5$ is an integer, so $x=1$ would not have found it. The odd term
$3x^{2}$ is what breaks parity, and it needs an even $x$ to show.)*

**D.** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}'(x)=\dfrac{4x^{3}+6x^{2}+2x}{4}=\dfrac{2x^{3}+3x^{2}+x}{2}=\dfrac{x(x+1)(2x+1)}{2}$,
which is an integer for every integer $x$ — again because $x(x+1)$ is even. The conclusion **holds**, so D
is not a counterexample.

**The lesson.** [Both halves must be checked, and in the cheap order]{.hl}: one substitution killed A and
B, and only then was it worth differentiating. *And when testing the conclusion, do not stop at $x=1$ — a
parity failure often needs an even input to appear.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 39 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A student is asked to prove whether the following statement $(*)$ is true or false:

> $(*)$ &nbsp; For all real numbers $a$ and $b$, &nbsp; $\lvert a+b\rvert<\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$

The student's proof is as follows:

> *Statement $(*)$ is **false**. A counterexample is $a=3$, $b=4$, as $\lvert3+4\rvert=7$ and
> $\lvert3\rvert+\lvert4\rvert=7$, but $7<7$ is false.*

Which of the following best describes the student's proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; $(*)$ is true, and the student's proof is not correct.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; $(*)$ is false, but the proof is not correct: the counterexample is not valid.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; $(*)$ is false, but the proof is not correct: the student needs to give **all** the values of $a$ and $b$ where $\lvert a+b\rvert<\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$ is false.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; $(*)$ is false, but the proof is not correct: the student should instead have stated that for all real $a$ and $b$, $\lvert a+b\rvert\le\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** &nbsp; $(*)$ is false, and the student's proof is fully correct.
:::

Every option except one accuses the student of something. [Before looking for the fault, check whether
there is one]{.hl}: does $a=3$, $b=4$ satisfy the hypothesis, and does it make the conclusion false?

Note the strict $<$ in $(*)$. The familiar triangle inequality has $\le$, and the difference is the whole
question.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — what a disproof is obliged to do, and what it is not
:::

**E — the statement is false, and the proof is fully correct.**

### The counterexample works

$a=3$ and $b=4$ are real numbers, so the hypothesis *"for all real $a$ and $b$"* covers them. And

$$\lvert3+4\rvert=7 ,\qquad \lvert3\rvert+\lvert4\rvert=3+4=7 ,\qquad 7<7 \text{ is false.}$$

So $(*)$ fails at this pair, and one failing case is enough to destroy a "for all" claim. **Nothing further
is required.**

### Why each accusation misses

| | the accusation | why it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $(*)$ is true | It is not: it fails at $a=3,b=4$, and indeed at every pair with the same sign. |
| **B** | the counterexample is invalid | It is valid — both numbers are real and the inequality genuinely fails. *The likely misreading is that $7<7$ being false somehow spoils it; that failure **is** the counterexample.* |
| **C** | you must list **all** failing values | No. *To disprove "for all", one case suffices; listing them all is a different and much larger task that nobody asked for.* |
| **D** | you should have written $\le$ instead | $\lvert a+b\rvert\le\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$ is a true statement, but the student was asked about $(*)$, not invited to repair it. *Replacing a claim with a nearby true one is not a proof or a disproof of the original.* |

### The mathematics behind it

$\lvert a+b\rvert=\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$ exactly when $a$ and $b$ have the same sign (or one is
zero); otherwise the strict inequality does hold. *So $(*)$ is not wildly false — it fails on precisely
half the plane, and $a=3,b=4$ is the simplest point in that half.*

**The lesson.** [A disproof owes you exactly one case, fully checked — no more]{.hl}. Options C and D are
both invitations to do unnecessary work, and both are wrong for the same reason: they mistake *thorough*
for *correct*. *When a question asks you to judge a proof, the answer "it is fine" is always on the table.*
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

## The one habit to leave with

Match the claim to the method on sight, and never prove a "for all" by examples. Contradiction and
counterexample carry the most marks on Paper 2 — the two to be fastest at. Part 3 is where the 8–9 marks
live: parity clashes, squares mod 4, extraneous roots.

And in Parts 4 and 5, before deciding whether a candidate is a counterexample, always ask the two questions
in this order: **does it satisfy the hypothesis**, and **does it break the conclusion**. Almost every wrong
answer in that bank is a candidate that fails the first question.
:::

:::
